utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just 15 seconds, if I may. Further tribute to Mr. Petkovic's ability to attract talented women to his Defence team, we have another intern starting with us today, Ms. Ashley Walker. I simply wanted to introduce her to the Court. We're delighted to have her on the Petkovic team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Let me say good morning to everyone here in this courtroom. Good morning to Ms. Ashley Walker, who is now a member of General Petkovic's Defence. I'm going to give the floor to the registrar who has two IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. 3D and 5D have submitted a list -- a response to the OTP objections regarding Defence exhibits tendered through Witness Bo Pellnas. The 3D list shall be assigned Exhibit number IC 605, while the 5D response shall be assigned Exhibit number IC 606. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I am going to give the floor now to Mr. Scott and we'll resume the examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; and good morning to everyone in the courtroom. In connection with our two newest members, I suppose we can never have enough talented women in the courtroom, so we welcome them to join us. Not enough talented men, but many talented women.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might go back a moment to a question that was raised -- if we could just pick up from yesterday and deal with a couple of matters, please. If you can look back at Exhibit 10058, which -- I see you don't have the binder yet.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, one of the -- one of the Defence counsel raised yesterday a question about this document, in particular on the last page, the last paragraph, which could be dealt with on cross-examination, I suppose redirect, but since it was raised, let me come back to it now. The language as pointed out to you in that paragraph, it says: "They were given the status of refugees." Now, in exploring this matter with you a bit -- just a bit more, can I refer you to your statement for further clarification, to paragraph 91 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 91 of your statement in connection with these men who had been released from Dretelj and had found themselves on Korcula, it says: "Dr. Granic," which is also explained in the same paragraph, and I think the Chamber and those in the courtroom may know by now, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia at the time, "Dr. Granic announced that it was agreed that once the detainees from Dretelj were released they would be accepted by Croatia and treated as guests of the country while waiting for further transit to third countries." Now, with that in mind and looking at the language in Dr. Kapetanovic's letter, which is Exhibit 10058, which you may want to go back to, if you see the letter, the language where Dr. Kapetanovic says, "They were given the status of refugees," my question to you really is: Was Dr. Kapetanovic correct in saying that? Were they in fact, to your knowledge, given refugee status at that time when they arrived on Korcula?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my knowledge tells me that they weren't given that status and could not have obtained it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission might I be allowed to request that since the Prosecutor has gone back to my observations that we take a look at when this meeting was in 1993. It says early in September, and it would be proper to say that Mr. Silajdzic attended the meeting too and the exhibit that the Prosecutor is presenting, 10058, let us just take a look at the date which the 9th of October, makes it one month difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried to deal with this matter briefly but I submit respectfully to the Chamber I think any further inquiry by counsel should be left to cross-examination. I would like to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further -- before going further from yesterday, madam, let me just ask you where we left off at the end of the day, I asked you a question; it was late in the day and perhaps my question wasn't clear. We were referring to exhibit -- which again may exist you to have in front of you. If you can turn to Exhibit 10067, which I believe is the last document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was a letter in which you mentioned, among other things, that you had written a letter and raised the matter that the number of -- you had contact with various people who had, at one time, been Dretelj detainees who had been released to Korcula and then sent on to other countries and that you were having contact with some of these people who were expressing a desire and making efforts to return to Bosnia. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my question -- the question that I asked you yesterday, and let me just restate my question and I'll try to clarify, I asked you -- I said given the number of issues that your embassy was dealing with around that time, and I'm -- for the purposes of the record, I'm now referring to pages 57 and 58 of yesterday's transcript. "Given the number of issues that your embassy was dealing with around that time, why did you find it noteworthy to send a report on this topic to your superiors and to the Ministry Of Foreign Affairs?" And let me clarify my question was not suggested to be critical of why the -- your department in Zagreb wasn't directly dealing with these issues at the time, and you explained that they would not have fallen within your area of responsibility at that time since they didn't relate to people who were then and there in Croatia, refugees in Croatia, as they were elsewhere, but why did you think that topic generally was important enough to bring to the attention of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sarajevo? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered that this was exceptionally important because they're the same former Dretelj detainees who sought all manner of ways and means to be allowed to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that because of their wish to return back home, they never ceased to maintain contact with the embassy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you then to go forward this morning. In reference to paragraph 62 of your -- I'm just making sure I'm not skipping something else. If I can direct your attention to the topics that are dealt with at paragraphs 62 to 64 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it. I've found those paragraphs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 63, you say that the refugees were losing the already-granted refugee status. In other words, in those instances where they had been granted refugee status. Most of these people who lost the status were in Zagreb, Split, Makarska. 64: "The newly arrived Bosnian Muslims were not given protection and could not get refugee status. They were coming from Herzegovina, which was under the HVO-controlled BiH territory." Can you say a bit more to the Judges about what you recall during this time period about refugee status either being -- that had already been given being revoked or not extended to persons newly arrived?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that a particular problem that we faced was with the Bosnian nationals with recognised refugee status who came from the area of Herzegovina -- or, rather, the territory under HVO control, because at that time the Office for Displaced persons and refugees issued a decree to their local offices saying that persons coming from Herzegovina should not have their refugee status extended because there wasn't a war going on there any more so that they forfeited their refugee status. Mostly the way they did this was they would be intercepted in the street and the police would take away their cards and the new arrivals weren't able to come by this refugee status at all. All the activities -- or, rather, the local offices referred back to the Dr. Adalbert Rebic decree and the Office for Displace Persons and Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apart from this indication that -- in line 10 today it says: "There wasn't a war going on there any more." Apart from that statement or basis, to your knowledge was any other justification or basis given for withdrawing or denying refugee status at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view there was no justification, and that includes this one to which the office referred, because at that time Bosnian nationals, Muslims, were not able to return to Herzegovina safely and securely. They were not able to return by land via Herzegovina to Bosnia, that is to say the other Muslim citizens either, because they ran the risk of facing the realistic danger of being arrested and detained by the HVO again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to paragraphs 65 through 67 in which you talk about something called the Rama action, in which you indicate that the Croatian Ministry of Interior arrested approximately 120 Bosnian Muslims to be deported back to BiH, Bosnia and Herzegovina. My only question to follow up on those paragraphs is did you ever receive any information on what happened to those 120 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can now direct your attention to paragraph 71 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While there is a pause and just going on: Madam, did you inquire about the fate of these 120 Muslims? Did you try to get information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We inquired through the system, contacted all the UN and other organisations present in Croatia asking for their assistance, asking that they become involved and try to find out what happened to those BH citizens. However, we never received an answer. And not to speculate on my part, I would assume that they didn't have that information either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I assume that they're going to produce some documents on this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We did not hear you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I assume that the lady has documents which would verify what she just indicated, that she made inquiries to all these organisations, something that we can at least look at tangibly and then verify and, if so, I assume she produced them to the Prosecution given that she's had three or four years' contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wanted to ask, madam, you have spoken of international organisations; did you also inquire with Croatian authorities, the MUP for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not personally, but through my consulate I did receive information which the consulate managed to obtain from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that information was, if any?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when I received information about the Rama operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, again if we could go to paragraph number 71. In paragraph 71 you deal again with the topic of some of these people being relocated on to Turkey, and you say: "Before people were sent to Turkey we offered them the possibility to go back to Bosnia," and then you give some further information about that, and you mention Tuzla again, and toward the end of that paragraph you say: "That is why we realised that we could enable them to leave only for Turkey." Let me just -- for purposes of clarification, can you just indicate to the Chamber again was it -- was it the preferred course of action? Was that your first choice, and not just yours personally but the first choice of the Bosnian government, that these people be transported to Turkey?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the last possibility, and we recognised it as such, to protect those citizens and to put them up in a safe area where they wouldn't be threatened from arrests and further persecution. So it wasn't the usual way of taking care of them or the reaction by the embassy or, rather, the department for displaced persons and refugees of the BH government in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps a similar thought but in case there might be a need for clarification, if you go to paragraph 75 of your statement. At the end of that paragraph you again -- you say: "I want to stress the fact that we organised the transport to Turkey only for those pushed to legal limbo." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand by that that we organised ourselves in the following way: We tried to talk individually to each of the BH citizens who wished to be -- who wished to go to Turkey to check and see whether they had recognised refugee status in Croatia or not. We primarily did not want to deal with the movement of refugees with refugee status. And we asked ourselves which UN organisation the citizens had contacted, and we sent them to the UNHCR first. And all those who confirmed that they were not able to receive protection from the UNHCR, because there were among them those who, under UNHCR protection, they knew -- actually, they knew that people protected by the UNHCR were also arrested and expelled. So this was done only on the basis of interviews and forms that they filled in and we would carry out selection in that way. We would choose individuals to join the group and to travel to Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you in this connection to look at Exhibit 4150.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We've looked at this document before, I believe, but just directing your attention to another part of the document, and I'm referring to the English translation, but if you look at the bottom -- toward the bottom of the third page, carrying over to the top of the following page. Does that document discuss again the question or the topic of moving various of these persons to Turkey?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to the English version. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Bottom of the third page.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. I've found the paragraph. And this relates to looking into the possibility of organised travel by BH citizens from Croatia to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in particular the topic of the movement to Turkey; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because we contacted the embassies of a number of countries, but it was only Turkey which replied and confirmed the fact that they were ready to take in these people, up to 2.000 BH citizens, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I next ask you to please go to Exhibit 10054.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that document is, please.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my letter, the department of refugees of the BH embassy in Zagreb, addressed to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in which in general terms -- no, I'm sorry. That doesn't seem to be it. It is a report from an official visit to Split between the 7th and 12th of September, 1993. That's what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And what was the occasion of your going to Split and Obonjan Island during the 7th to 12th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report, I state the main reason for the visit, which was the very difficult situation in the refugee centre on the island of Obonjan, the plight of the refugees. And in the letter I go on to explain that we viewed the complexity of the situation on Obonjan and the fact that we understood why the citizens -- or, rather, refugees from BH accommodated on Obonjan Island were constantly sending in requests for help and assistance, and to enable them to go further on to other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the second page of the English version, about the middle of the page, just to follow up on some questions that came up yesterday. If you find the paragraph, please, that starts, "Like in other refugee centres ..."

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Like in other refugee centres, most of our citizens have no identification papers. Representatives of the embassy ... visited the island at the beginning of August 1993. At that time, collective passports were issued to the citizens of Mostar and everybody else who was interested." And you -- we discussed collective passports yesterday. And then you go on to say: "The collective passports were issued to the citizens of Mostar because they were in transit through the Republic of Croatia. We had no information about how the host country was going to treat them, so we began preparations, as an emergency measure, for their collective relocation." And is that, in fact, an accurate report of the state of affairs at the time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to page 5 of the English version. It's the last paragraph preceding the section heading II.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The third line of that paragraph it says -- makes reference to closing down the refugee centre on the island. And we're talking about Obonjan now, I take it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the passage in front of me. I'm looking at page 5, above II. Is that the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct. In the third line of that paragraph it makes reference to: "closing down the refugee centre on the island." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just simply tell us whether that refugee centre or camp on that island was closed down any time around this time, that is, the fall, let's say, of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up until my return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is August 1994, the refugee centre had not been closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 78 of your statement -- paragraph 78 of your statement you make this statement which I would like you then to add to or further explain if you're able, please. "We realised that the Croatian authorities were waiting for such a good opportunity to start moving refugees from other parts of Croatia to Obonjan and Gasinci, the two worst places for the refugees to be. As Croatian authorities expected, refugees tried everything to leave the country." Now, can you explain to the Judges more what was happening here, what you mean by this part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant to say by this part of the statement was that it was well known that at the moment when refugees would be moved from previous refugee centres or private accommodation where they were staying, when they would be moved from Obonjan or to Gasinci, the refugees would start looking at all conceivable ways of leaving the Republic of Croatia. Both places had their specific characteristics, and it was quite understandable to me why people did not want to spend any amount of time at these places. Do you want me to give more details about these specific characteristics?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific characteristic of the collecting centre at Gasinci was this location. It was right next to training grounds of the regular Croatian army, including heavy weaponry. This was an open message as far as the refugees were concerned because often the guns of this weaponry were turned to the camp. Very often policemen would enter the camp, arrest them there. There were even physical beatings of the refugees. The general atmosphere was more than disturbing. It could be characterised as hysterical at certain points of time when I visited them. As for the island of Obonjan, the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina are people from the continent, from the land. Mostly they were elderly people, women or elderly, frail men who had never moved from their homes before. So living on an island was stressful enough for them. It was something that they were not used to. Also, there were former criminals staying at the island too. I already mentioned yesterday that there were psychopaths and murders among them who were waiting for deportation to Bosnia-Herzegovina once they have served their sentences. Then there were members of the special police force of the Republic of Croatia. As for the Bosnian citizens who were staying at the island, they were terrified of these special police forces. Also, what was very hard for them was the fact that they could not go to land when they wanted to, the mainland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that. May I then move us forward to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a question to get a bit more colour if possible. Are you aware, madam, whether there have been any crimes committed by these ex-convicts that had been brought to the island to the detriment of refugees, or was it just an abstract fear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, they did not act to the detriment of refugees. However, I personally came across two of these former ex-convicts. It is practically with a sense of pride that they spoke about their crimes, the crimes that they had committed, and I asked whether they had contact with refugees and whether they told the refugees about what it was that they had done, and they said that it was only natural that they could meet with refugees and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope other than colour we will get some proof. I think proof is what we need as opposed to colour. This is all anecdotal. I assume that the young -- that the woman has proof in documents that she submitted, or investigations. I think that's what we need in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam, just a question. What you're saying might be a bit confusing, and I believe that we must absolutely shed light on what you're saying. So those convicts, those criminals who were there waiting to be sent back to Bosnia, BiH, when you said that, you know, it struck me because I was thinking about the Cubans that had been transferred to centres in Miami where there was a mix of criminals and refugees. I thought this is what you were hinting at. Then while listening to you I started to wonder whether those criminals -- "criminals" weren't nationals from BiH that had than tried by courts in Croatia and that were actually serving their sentence while they were waiting to be transferred back to their own country. So these so-called criminals, could you tell us what category they belonged to? Were they nationals of BiH that had been tried in Croatia and that were supposed to go back to their country to serve, finish their sentence, or were they just people that had been coming in with the influx of refugees among which there were these criminal elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were persons who had been convicted of having committed different crimes in the former Yugoslavia. They were serving their sentences in some of the prisons in Croatia. Once they had served their sentences, Croatia did not return them to Bosnia-Herzegovina in view of the war operations. Rather, they were all relocated to Obonjan until they were returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for their stay in Obonjan, I sent letters about that to the UNHCR and other organisations, always asking for some kind of help. What comes to mind right now is a particular situation when there was a number of ex-convicts among them together with some refugees who were in Obonjan, and according to the information provided by refugees, they were deported to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then I sent letters stating the actual number of persons who were taken from Obonjan, thus seeking protection for these people and asking for information to be sent to us about what came out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you right, madam, there were several categories. You had those who had been convicted during the times of former Yugoslavia and who were serving their sentence in Croatian prisons but who were BiH nationals and who were supposed to go back to BiH because -- now that BiH had become independent. Since they were prisoners of BiH they were supposed to go back there to serve their sentence. But you seem to also be saying that in the influx of refugees, there were some individuals which had been convicted in BiH and that had just mingled in with the refugees. So all together there were several categories in terms of criminals. Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry if I wasn't specific enough. To the best of my knowledge, all of them were convicts who had been convicted in the time of the former Yugoslavia. They served many years in prison. Many of them had served 10 or 15 or 20 years. They were set free in the period from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia had already been recognised since due to these new facts they had become nationals of a country that was at war, Croatian did not send them to Bosnia-Herzegovina straight away. They kept them at the island of Obonjan officially until conditions were created for their return to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You were extremely detailed. Mr. Scott, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could then direct your attention on to paragraph 90 of your statement. This is a paragraph, madam, where you deal with the fact that you had some conversations with a person you identify as a priest from Citluk.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us at the end of the day, so to speak, did you consider that this request was actually to assist these Muslims who were being referred to here, or how did you understand the request that was being made of you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I was very, very worried. There were several telephone contacts. At first I thought that this was sincere concern about the Muslims who were under threat in the area. However, the gentleman who introduced himself as Nedeljko Galic seemed more and more insincere to me. And in response to my question as to whether he had any possibility to help them go to Bosnia-Herzegovina if they wish, he said that they heard that it was cold in Bosnia, there was no food in Bosnia. He helped me make my decision, because I thought that this kind of approach could not be sincere as far as I was concerned or as far as the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina was concerned. Is there a single citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina who needs to hear that it was cold in Bosnia? So I characterised him as insincere straight away, and I didn't go back to that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going forward, then, to deal with the question of again the refugees and the people that found themselves in Croatia. If I can ask you to look at paragraph 102. And you make reference in that paragraph to a copy of instructions sent by Mr. Rebic's office to regional offices in Croatia. The document said that the refugee status is to be terminated for those coming from so-called "safe areas," in other words, Mostar, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, Pocitelj, and other places under HVO control. When and how, generally, did you first come to know of the existence of these instructions from Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I give an answer, I will put a question. The interpreter said "safe areas," but I wanted to have this corrected into "safe areas."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Different words in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of contacts, regardless of whether it was refugees who were coming to the office and whether they were phoning us seeking help, assistance as to how they should behave in a situation when their refugee status was not being extended. We tried to establish official contact with Mr. Rebic's office seeking clarification, but we never got an official answer. However, our refugees helped us get a copy of the document, namely a copy of the decree that the office for refugees and displaced persons from Zagreb had sent to all of their regional offices, and this decree pertained to the following: Citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are from the towns of Mostar, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, Pocitelj, and others under the control of the HVO should not have their refugee status extended. Refugees realised that they could not return to these areas, that they did not have any protection, that they would remain totally unprotected, and of course they sought advice from the embassy -- or, rather, concrete help to have their problem resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the witness did not respond to the question. My colleague's question was when and how she first came to know, et cetera. We didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think we heard the how. On the basis of contacts, regardless of whether it was refugees, et cetera. So that answer is given. As to the when, I'm sure that in the next few minutes and with exhibits it will become very clear. So I think it's -- I think the witness has indeed gone a bit ahead of us and answered my next question, but if you really want me to ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you hear? You were proceeding to answer it, madam.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically I heard that there was a new problem, that refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina were not having their refugee status extended and that their status was not regulated in terms of their further stay in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to go to paragraph 103 of your -- the next paragraph of your statement. You indicated that you met with Mr. Rebic and raised your concerns with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise for interrupting. My learned friend said a few moments ago that we would get the answer as to "when" a bit later, and now he is directing the witness to paragraph 103 when there is no time reference again. We still don't know. Was it in 1991? No problem. 1994, no problem, but 1993 could be somewhat different. You know full well through these proceedings as my colleague knows as well that from month-to-month the situation in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Croatia, was changing dramatically. So time is of essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, could you tell us the approximate date you learned this? Could you give us a date when you knew -- when you finally found out about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to try to remember, because I know that there are minutes from meetings and different documents, my reports, that are all dated. I think it would be better if the Prosecutor would help us find the right documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I was allowed to go to the next exhibit it would be clear. And also, I would have assumed that when I directed the courtroom's attention to paragraph 103, I had assumed that people would have read paragraph 100, which says: "From September 1993 onwards, until the end of my mission on the 31st of August, that Mr. Rebic," and so on. And the first document, Your Honour -- can we just get to the document that says 31 October 1993? Why are we wasting time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go, please, Witness, to document 100059?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Kovacic, I think it would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Then I will not and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it is better to have some patience, and you will have a lot time in cross-examination in case you are not satisfied now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, of course. I shall be patient and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you asked me, but sometimes when we're patient, I have to take you 15 minutes back and by then nobody knows what it was we had been talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, if you have Exhibit 10059 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have Exhibit 10059, can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter of the embassy of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb sent to the office for expellees and refugees of the government of the Republic of Croatia. It was written by the department for refugees. I can see that on the basis of the number of the protocol. The date is the 31st of October, 1993. Through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs along with this note a document was sent to Mr. Rebic and his office, and this letter requests the office for expellees and refugees of the government of the Republic of Croatia to provide an explanation in view of refugees -- actually, I prefer reading this. "Refugees are given the following explanation: That the conditions have been created for their return to the safe areas, Mostar and others, and therefore they lose their refugee status in Croatia. Social care centres explain that this is based on a decision made by the government of the Republic of Croatia, rather, the office for refugees and expellees." So I wrote this in October 1993 through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I seek an answer from the Office for Expellees and Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention on to Exhibit 10060. That should be the next document in your binder. Did you in fact receive -- you or the embassy receive a response from Mr. Rebic dated the 4th of November? There's one date at the top of the letter, but if you look at the 4th of November, 1993. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that letter Mr. Rebic reports -- the second paragraph in the letter. It says: "We hereby inform you that the office has issued a directive to its regional offices and relevant social welfare centres on the revoking of the refugee status for persons who have residence in war-free zones. The office has also issued a directive that the refugee status should be extended for persons who are unable to go home because their houses are destroyed, et cetera, until the conditions for their return are met." Now, a few minutes ago you were saying it had come to your attention that this directive had gone out. And is the information reflected in Mr. Rebic's letter of the 4th of November, 1993, is that consistent with the information that you had received around this time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. As for not extending the status of refugees to persons from Stolac, Mostar, et cetera, it is consistent. I did not see a document where it is stated that those who cannot return because their houses were destroyed should have their status continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any interaction with refugees or persons, displaced persons, in Croatia who had indicated that they had tried, for example, to take advantage of what we might call the second clause, just my characterisation, and say, "Well, yes we understand we have been told to go back but my house was destroyed or whatever; for various reasons I can't go back." Did you run into any persons or have any encounters or conversations with persons who addressed that aspect?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contacts with persons who in the wish of obtaining necessary documentation on the basis of which they could have their refugee status extended asked what it was that they had to do, and they realised that most of the original documents they needed, they could get only in the municipalities that they came from. This was an enormous problem for them, and I knew why, because that meant that they physically had to return to the places that they had been expelled from themselves physically, and they didn't dare do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm reading the letters you've drafted and the answer sent to you by the government of the Republic of Croatia through Mr. Rebic. On the basis of these documents, the Croatian authorities seem to be about to pass two directives -- to issue two directives, one of them related to refugees who are losing their refugee status because the areas where they hail from have been pacified. Calm has been restored in these areas, war is not raging any more, and therefore these people are in a position to go home. And the second directive could be related to people who can't go back home because their houses have been destroyed. And the second directive would give them the refugee status, would extend the refugee status to them. Is that what you understood when reading Mr. Rebic's letter, and was the situation amongst refugees consistent with what we see in this document, an official document from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was terribly surprised by the information set out in the letter by Dr. Adalbert Rebic, I insisted and managed to organise a meeting with Mr. Adalbert Rebic, and at that meeting I asked him quite openly who could have had this idea of revoking the status of Bosnia and Herzegovinian citizens, Muslims, and forcing them back to areas under HVO control, where the same fate would have befallen them, incarceration or expulsion. Or, rather, that with this decree they were forced to remain without regulated status in Croatia and once again open to the possibility of being arrested by the Croatian police. And then I received precise explanation from Dr. Adalbert Rebic, to the effect that they had in mind refugees who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were Croats who had fled from those areas and who now began to use their refugee status as spending time in their weekend cottages before they went back to their homes and took up their normal way of life again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I would like to ask a question regarding the document, particularly the original or, rather, the one in B/C/S, because it is not the original. It seems to be from a -- from a collection of documents, and what strikes me is that we have two dates on the English version, 4 of December and then 4 of November, and I do not understand what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to come back and clarify some of the points in the last few minutes but to answer Your Honour, the documents that were turned over, were turned over by way of a diskette, computer diskette, so when they were downloaded, if you will, they were downloaded and printed in this fashion, and I'm sure the witness can confirm that further. As to the error of the particular date, I can't explain it any more than an error. But in term of the format of the document, I think the witness can confirm to the Chamber the nature in which the B/C/S documentation was provided in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, can you explain to the Judges why the -- some of the B/C/S -- some of the B/C/S documents, not all of them, but some of them that we've looked at yesterday, and perhaps today, are in the format they are in?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the department for refugees, and probably in other departments of the BH embassy in Croatia, had the possibility on an electronic format to send out mail, e-mail, to the department dealing with encryption and sending out information from Zagreb to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. So that the difference in dates, it be quite logical. Possibly it was the case that on the 4th of December I sent out information to Sarajevo about dates -- about documents which had other dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I go on for a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What puzzles me a bit is that in the English translation there is reference to a handwritten mention on the original, "104425". And I do not find that in -- in the B/C/S version nor any mention of a rukabis [phoen] or something. It is just a bit -- a bit puzzling. Do you have an explanation for that? And then, Mr. Karnavas -- you have an explanation, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think -- I don't know if I have a total explanation, but as I understand it, the witness has her own collection, her own archive, which she put on a disk and provided to the Prosecution. And she may have also had hard copies. So I assume that's how it -- that's how it happened, which then begs the question: Is her archive a complete archive? Is this part of the archive that she gave to -- for instance, to the ambassador because she makes mention of that -- of that in her own report. So these are the sort of explanations that I think do deserve to be answered, because who knows what else she may have that she's not providing, like personal notes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your interests are not the same as mine, Mr. Karnavas, I can see that and understand it and accept it. But it seems that the translator had a different copy than the one we have here, and this I find needy of explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy to make -- I'll be happy to make further inquiry about it. I have -- I have an educated guess as to what happened, but I don't know if I should make that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Wait till you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Some of these documents were turned over by another witness, and it is often the case -- it is often the case when an investigator in the field, I think properly so, takes documents from a witness, there is some notation made to make a record of the document being handed over on that day. And while I don't have the specific information in front of me, I suspect, I emphasise the word "suspect," that the number that you've indicated was handwritten on another document was such a number for purposes of reference, but I can certainly make further inquiry, Your Honour. That's as far as I can take it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the witness does not dispute that these -- that the papers we have before us correspond essentially to the originals and that might then do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute about that, and I would think it rather old fashioned, and I'm often accused of being a bit old fashioned, I suppose, but in this day of electronic records and computers, that the fact that someone would print this out from a diskette would not be something the witness can confirm as, yes, this is a copy of the letter -- this is the letter that I sent on such-and-such a date previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, if we could please go forward then to Exhibit 07 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Mr. Scott. Because of these documents we've lost track of the answer given by the witness in relation to the two decrees and in relation to the answer given by Mr. Rebic. If I understand you correctly, Mr. Rebic, whom you asked questions about this letter, told you, allegedly told you, that this letter only related to BiH Croats who were amongst the refugees, and therefore Mr. Rebic was of the mind that these people should go home because they were spending just too much time there. In other words, this letter of a general import, this letter was related only to Croats and not to Muslims. Is that really what you intended to say when you gave your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I wanted to say, that the decree was one written in general terms and referred to all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas his oral explanation was that he meant just the BH Croats, whose time had come to return home.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but now the logical question is whether the witness saw the decree, because we didn't -- we don't know whether she saw it or not. Can we ask her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see these two decrees? Did Mr. Rebic give you a copy? Are you familiar with these documents or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking about one set of instructions. Mr. Adalbert Rebic didn't give it to me, but I received it from the other departments. I read it and reacted to it, and that's why I organised this meeting with Mr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the letter, in the last paragraph, Mr. Rebic seems to be saying that he sent the two directives to your embassy. I'd like you to turn your attention to the last paragraph of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take a look at the footnote where I explain that I looked through the entire protocol of all the letters coming into the embassy and took note that that letter never arrived at the embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me follow up this various -- these various questions going back to what -- something you said earlier. You've indicated the explanation given to you by Mr. Rebic was that at least for the most part this directive was intended, in his view, for application to Bosnian Croats who were living essentially on the Dalmatian coast and could then return to HVO-controlled areas, but is that -- despite what Mr. Rebic told you on that occasion, was that the experiences of the refugees and displaced persons in of -- of Muslim ethnicity, is that what they were actually experiencing as the reports -- according to the reports you received?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single BH citizen who was a Croat contacted me, but Muslims did, who knew that they could not and did not dare return. I knew this because it was only BH Muslim citizens who came to see me who weren't able to obtain an extension of their refugee status.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to go to Exhibit 7022. Madam, Exhibit 07022 is a letter from someone named Martin Raguz to Mr. Rebic dated the 3rd of December, 1993. Did Mr. Rebic ever tell -- you said earlier -- I believe you said -- excuse me. I believe you made reference a few moments ago that the information as to what would be considered the safe areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina according to someone, that information was coming from someone in Herceg-Bosna, or what did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Did Mr. -- let me come at it this way. Did you hear anything further from Mr. Rebic after meeting with him and raising these issues about any further steps that were being taken to deal with the issue you raised, and whether there were any communications between Mr. Rebic and HVO officials in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information at all about whether which there were any communications and talks between Mr. Adalbert Rebic and the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me come back to it then in a moment or two. Before we go to that -- deal with that exhibit further, then, can I ask you to go to Exhibit 10062.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, in response to the point that you made earlier, this document in particular is essentially a compilation of a series of exchange of correspondence which has been translated as one document, and again if you look at the B/C/S original, you'll see that again, a number of documents have been printed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, madam. Is it correct -- do we understand correctly that in the B/C/S version of these documents what has happened is a number of letters have been essentially, how everyone wants to put it, downloaded or printed as a series on one continuous document, if you will?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding of these documents that were on -- in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to turn to that particular document that's included in this series of letters as the item that is dated, and in the English version -- in the English version it is dated the 19th of February, and on the third -- of 1994, on the fourth page of the English materials. And in the B/C/S version, I'm afraid you will have to assist me, but if you could please turn to that component which is dated -- also dated the 19th of February, 1994, to Mr. Rebic. "Dear Mr. Rebic." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date here is the 6th of February, 1994. Is that the document we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me double-check again myself, please. My apology. My error. Can I ask you to look at the document that -- the item that is dated the 14th of February, 1994? It should be the second document. The set of materials starts with the letter dated the 6th of February, "Dear Mr. Rebic." Then it goes on. The next item is 14th of February, 1994, "Dear Ms. Turkovic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about this question a few moments ago and that's the reason I've directed you to this particular document. And Mr. Rebic is writing to the ambassador, Ms. Turkovic, at this time and says how the safe -- so-called -- well, what some have called, or the terminology that was used was "safe areas", or areas that were safe, and Mr. Rebic says: "Dear Mrs. Turkovic. I have to inform you that the office of the government for the Republic of Croatia For Expelled Persons And Refugees is not able to identify the crisis areas in the neighbouring Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For that reason, we have acted in compliance with the guidelines issued by the office of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for expelled persons and refugees, attached hereto. "Based on the guidelines issued by the said office, the whole sub-Neretva region and the following areas in Western Herzegovina have been declared as safe: "Livno, Duvno, Grude, Ljubuski, Capljina, Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Pocitelj, Medjugorje ..." et cetera. "Therefore, the status of refugees is no longer recognised, i.e., has been revoked ..." Now, can you confirm that is a letter that the embassy received from Mr. Rebic explaining how that determination was made?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is the letter, and it is also correct that the letter provides information on the basis of which the decree was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you discussed these matters, and going back to the meeting that you made reference to a few minutes ago, to your meeting with Mr. Rebic, was there any discussion whether going back to these areas was safe for Croats or safe for Muslims or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. Just a point of clarification. When was the initial meeting? Because this document refers to in February now. So it would seem, at least for -- you know, since this situation was very fluid, and I think the meeting was held the previous year, perhaps we can be clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll refer back in the record to the testimony already given. The first document that we looked at was 10059 which was dated the 31st of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so the question now that she's being asked now relates to the situation in February. And so if she's going to give an answer, based on a meeting that she had months earlier, given the fluidity of the situation, I don't think it's proper. I think unless he's going to ask her if she had a meeting with respect to this particular period of time. That was my point, but now I think that we've clarified it, if she just wants to take a wild guess, that's fine, but there's no foundation upon which she can answer this question, related to this particular document at this particular time, based on a meeting that she held months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I would have assumed that in preparation counsel will have read the statement. On paragraph 100, the same one I referred to before, the witness introduces this entire topic by stating, and I'll read it again: "From September 1993 onwards until the end of my mission on 31st August 1994, Mr. Rebic contacted us in order to get a list of safe zones in BiH to which BiH refugees could be repatriated from Croatia." This was an ongoing, and what's indicated from that, and from the documents we've looked at before and additional documents we have yet to look at, is that this was an ongoing series of communications from the fall of 1993 into 1994, as this issue was continuing and ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that they had ongoing communication, but the question related to a meeting. A meeting is different from communications. Had Mr. Scott laid down the proper foundation, a predicate: Did you have a meeting with Mr. Rebic at or about this period of time in relation to this particular topic? If the answer is yes, then: What, if anything, did you learn from Mr. Rebic concerning this, and so on and so forth. That was my concern. Whether they had communications, that's not an issue, but the question related to a meeting. That's what caused my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas created the need for a meeting. What if they didn't meet? What if they sent court letters to each other, what if they talked on the telephone? Where is it in the rules of evidence that the only way that one communicates information from one person to another is in a meeting. Come on, why are we wasting time on this? There is an exchange of correspondence; the documents are in front of Your Honours which all of you can read. And the witness has been explaining that correspondence in detail to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 15 seconds, madam, we are talking about a letter dated February 1994, 14th of February, 1994. Before this letter, did you have a meeting with Mr. Rebic or did you only have contacts with him on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I discussed this at the meeting that we mentioned, and we saw document -- a document about that meeting. And at that meeting Mr. Rebic himself agreed with me that the decree was rather cynical because it applied to BH Muslim citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But if we look at the letter of the month of February, the meeting had taken place months before that letter when Mr. Rebic proved extremely cynical. That was several months earlier than the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same situation applied to this period too. But after my meeting with Mr. Rebic, there were periods in which they extended the status of BH Muslim citizens. Then they would stop doing that. Then they would continue to extend the status, and their behaviour varied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. It's half past 10.00. We need to have a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may resume. You may resume, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, in the interest of time, I'd like to move on to the next exhibit unless there's any questions from the Judges continuing from before the break. I would like to -- in this continuing series of communications on this issue or topic, let me next ask you to go, please, to 8160. When you have document, could you just briefly tell us what that is and how that fits into the series of communications between the Bosnian embassy in Zagreb and Mr. Rebic on this issue during this time period -- continuing time period?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these instructions, the government of the Republic of Croatia, the Office for Refugees and Expellees, is abolishing refugee status to persons from the BiH: Mostar. Refugee status is abolished to all persons from Mostar who have such status recognised in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. And through this document the government of Croatia claims that it is possible to return to Mostar starting the 1st of April, 1994, and this pertains to all persons who from Mostar and who have a personal file marked, "Refugee". It is general. It has no particular reference to age, gender, or the status refugees have in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I then turn your attention to Exhibit 10063.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just confirm to us that this is a letter sent by Ambassador Turkovic to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sarajevo on the -- again, I think we have another -- excuse me for one moment. No, I'm sorry. The 2nd of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After quoting the letter received -- or the information received from Mr. Rebic, if you go to the second page of -- in the English version. Or in the Bosnian version the -- anyway, it's the first text following the extended quotation of material. In the English version, it will be on the second page under the words where it says "unquote." My question to you, madam, is that the report to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs says: "The directive has been circulated to all regional offices and social welfare centres, and they started acting on it immediately." And was that in fact the information you had and were receiving at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you go on in the letter -- or, well, you -- did you prepare this particular letter for the ambassador? Perhaps you can tell. It's not a major point, but ...

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am also aware of the content of this letter, but it also has the code from the embassy in Zagreb. That was 04.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then do you go on in your letter -- I'm not to go through all the paragraphs now and partly in the interest of time, but you report in this a number of the problems this is causing for the Muslim refugees in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before leaving this document, could I ask you to go to -- further on in the document starts a series of numbered paragraphs. Well, it's a further series. There are several sets of numbered paragraphs, but if you get to the part of the document that says "Note," n-o-t-e, another series of numbers start. If I can ask you to go to paragraph number 5 of that series. At the end of that paragraph it says: "One of the official written explanations was that the refugee status was revoked on the basis of Instruction issued by the 'Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.'" And touching back on something that we talked about earlier this morning, do you recall any more information about the instruction received from Herceg-Bosna on this topic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I really have nothing to say. Perhaps I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I just asked if you were having -- if you could give us -- recall anything further about that, but I'll move on. If I can ask you to go to -- please? Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is one passage which I find interesting. It is said in the note 5 that -- about the middle of that paragraph: "One of the official written explanations was that the refugee status was revoked on the basis of Instruction issued by the 'Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.'" I wonder, Witness, whether you could explain who was the addressee of such instructions? Instructions given to whom by authorities of CRHB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my understanding from Mr. Rebic's letter that was sent to the embassy to Mrs. Turkovic. We discussed it this morning before the break. However, in direct communication with Mr. Rebic, I reminded him that he certainly knew that there were no instructions that he received from the officially recognised state of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that he could not act in accordance with any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have not exactly answered my question. Instructions given to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regional offices of the office for refugees and expellees of the government of Republic of Croatia in Zagreb. They had their regional offices in Split and all other places, bigger towns in the Republic of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it not rather surprising? How do you explain that an authority of the Republic of Herceg-Bosnia gives instructions to Croatian authorities in a different republic? Did you take this up with someone? Did it strike you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this was not really understood properly. The Office for expellees and refugees of the government of Croatia issued instructions to their own regional offices on the basis of the decree or instructions that it got from the government of the HZ HB. That is what they were invoking, their decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, based on your question though she hasn't answered the question. One of the official written explanations. Written by whom? Who gave that explanation? She talks about an instruction. Where is the instruction? She was a member of that particular embassy so obviously she would have had that instruction handy. Somebody would have given it to her if that instruction existed. So where is this official written explanation that somebody issued an instruction, or is this merely an embellishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not. And the record, I thought, was fairly clear on this but I fear, now, we will have to spend quite a bit of additional time repeating some of the testimony from before the break. The evidence was that Mr. Rebic issued his instructions to the -- as the head of the Croatian ODPR to the field offices of ODPR and to the social welfare centres. That was mentioned both by the witness and in exhibits that we went through this morning. Then following that there was an exchange of correspondence and questions and communication with this witness and perhaps Ms. Turkovic as well, in which Mr. Rebic himself indicated that he had done this on the basis of information received from Herceg-Bosna. And we went through that correspondence this morning, and now we're moving on further and that is a series of events. Not the in -- not that there was instruction issued to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there was an instruction for information conveyed from Herceg-Bosna to the Republic of Croatia. I do think that apparently some things seem to be confused. If we need to go back through the documents again, I will do so. If you look back at Exhibit 10062, starting with the letter dated the 14th of February, 1994, Mr. Rebic in his letter on the third page of Exhibit 10062, which we looked at earlier this morning, Mr. Rebic says: "Based on the guidelines issued by the said office," and he says before that, let me back up. My apology. Let me back up. "Dear Mrs. Turkovic, the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia. "Dear Mrs. Turkovic, I have to inform you that the office of the government for the Republic of Croatia for expelled persons and refugees is not able to identify the crisis areas in the neighbouring Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For that reason we have acted in compliance, in compliance with the guidelines issued by the office of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for expelled persons and refugees. Based on the guidelines issued by said office ... " et cetera. That is Mr. Rebic's letter, setting out directly where that information and guidance for compliance came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have an objection to that, Your Honour. There's a difference between guidelines and instructions and I think that's what caught my attention, and I'm glad it caught your attention as well because there's a difference; there is a distinction between guidelines and instructions. So with that clarification, if we understand what is being mentioned here are guidelines rather than instructions, then, fine. Otherwise, I would like instructions being produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Continuing on, madam, in that same Exhibit 10062, to follow up on the question raised by Judge Trechsel, I knew it was in the document but I was hoping to save time against my limited time, maybe the Chamber will grant me some flexibility on this, if you go -- if you find in that same document, madam, the next item which is dated the 19th of February, 1994, which is a letter from Ambassador Turkovic in response, again, to Mr. Rebic, the 19th of February, 1994. The fourth page of the English materials. "Dear Mr. Rebic. Thank you for your letter of 14th of February, 1994." So I can hope we can all see this appears to be a response to the letter we looked at just a few moments ago which is dated the 14th of February 1994. "This letter has prompted us to review our previous correspondence." Now, in that letter, going on to the second page of that letter, which is overall page number 5 of the English materials and, madam, to try to assist you, it is in the B/C/S, Bosnian language version, it would be the sixth, if the paragraphs were the same, it would be in the sixth paragraph of the letter.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador Turkovic says to Mr. Rebic: "In your letter of 14 February 1994, you say that the refugees from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina staying in the Republic of Croatia are being dealt with in compliance with the guidelines issued by the office of the so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for expelled persons and refugees, and that these guidelines were attached to the letter. However, this embassy has not received them." It goes on to say: "Acting in compliance with the guidelines ..." et cetera, et cetera. And then further following up on the question first raised by Judge Trechsel some minutes ago, if you go to page 6 of the English materials and, madam, if you can find paragraph of Ambassador Turkovic's letter which starts with the word -- several paragraphs down from the one we just looked at, about two, starting with the words, "Since the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." Do you see that? Tell me when you have it, please?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador Turkovic responds: "Since the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the only international recognised state, any instruction coming from the institution of the so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna cannot serve as a legal basis for the internationally recognised states to issue their guidelines for regulating the status of refugees." Now, is all that in the exchange of correspondence between Ambassador Turkovic and Mr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's save time, because I don't think we should spend the whole day on this. These instructions or those guidelines or -- your embassy never got them; right? This is what the ambassador seems to say. You never saw these instructions or guidelines or whatever they're called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not receive these instructions given by the HZ HB. We received the letter of Mr. Rebic where he invokes these instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So nobody ever received these instructions, ever saw these instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The embassy? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, let's further -- let's go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to continue the series of correspondence, hopefully quite quickly. If I can ask you then to go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can give me one moment, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. I lost track myself exactly before all that, the last exhibit we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, if I could next ask you to look at Exhibit 10064.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'd just simply like to confirm with you that this is a similar -- well, strike the word "similar." This is a letter sent by Ambassador Turkovic to a number of international organisations also dealing with this same issue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next to go to 8195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on this -- on the document we just had, on the first page, the first paragraph -- no, the last paragraph on the page in the English. It's the second paragraph. "The directive was apparently issued on 30 April 1994 ..." Is that correct when the letter is dated 6 April 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We mentioned that the instructions were allegedly adopted on the 30th of April -- or, rather, dated the 30th of April, 1994, and that this was applied from the 1st of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But with due respect, you are writing three weeks, four weeks earlier almost. It must be an error, isn't it? Should it read -- what should it read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that this is a typographical error. However, I would have to read this properly in order to be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there must have been a second typographical error to say the least if the instructions which were made on the 30th of April were being implemented in effect from the 1st of April. Perhaps Your Honour would like to ask a follow-up question to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy, but I do not think that is necessary. It's too obvious that we -- this must be back in March at the latest, 30th March. Please proceed Mr. Scott, and excuse me for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. I appreciate it. I was just looking myself. I do think we had an earlier document on point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That seems to be the case, because Document P 8160 states that these instructions had been issued on March 30th, 1994, for application as of April 1st, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Mindua. That's exactly -- I was just turning to exactly the same document. Thank you very much. So 30th of March, 30th of April, but in any event, this one says clear as of 1st of April, 1994, and we did look at that document earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe we are about to turn to 8195 before that, if we could, please. I asked you -- as you're looking for that madam, I asked you earlier this morning, and since that is ongoing situation that's covering a period of some months as has been pointed out, despite the various correspondence and explanations perhaps that were going between Mr. Rebic and your embassy, were you continuing to get -- did you continue to get reports from the field, if you will, about Muslims in Croatia being harassed or having their refugee status or otherwise their status revoked or otherwise coming into difficulty?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the subject matter that this letter of the office for refugees pertains to. It was signed by Ambassador Turkovic on the 14th of April, 1994. This deals with a series of problems that the refugees have to confront.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to stop on the third paragraph, the middle of that letter, do you see where it says: "However, we have been informed by refugees from Mostar who are currently staying in Split and Sibenik area, that their refugee cards are being revoked and that they are not receiving food vouchers any longer by which actions they are forced to go to Mostar or a third country." And can you confirm that that was the reports and information that your embassy was receiving at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can next ask you to go to document 10 -- excuse me, 10066.
