utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a letter again from Ambassador Turkovic, dated the 16th of April, 1994. In the first paragraph numbered 1 it says: "Despite an agreement reached on 11 April 1994." Do you recall what that agreement -- if there in fact, one, was there an agreement, and, two, what was that agreement about?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreement was certainly reached at a meeting or, rather, the meeting that I mentioned in this letter. However, I cannot respond straight away as to what this was all about. I would have to go through the document a bit in order to be able to do that. Obviously there was an official meeting, and we issued a press release about it afterwards as to how the instruction on abolishing the status of refugees would be applied, that is to say, the one that pertained to the citizens of Mostar. What we assert here is that it is not taking place in accordance with the agreement and also in terms of what the press release said. We are informing Professor Rebic about the fact that BH citizens continue to inform us about the problems that they have with their refugee status. It is stated here that yet again we were in touch with Professor Adalbert Rebic, asking him to abide by the agreement reached at the meeting held on the 11th of April. The letter also refers to concrete examples; BH citizens, Mrs. Emina Novo, Mehmed Pasalic, who were refugees from Mostar. Reference is made to the problems that they had. They had problems with the Croatian police. Ah, I see. A problem was created by the Croatian police, because they did not have personal IDs issued by the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, or they did not have a domovnica. Then we also quoted here a document that was the statement of the Split regional office for refugees and expellees. The content of this document was quoted in full in order to inform the Foreign Ministry. I don't know who we sent this to. I seem to be a bit lost now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To the ministry.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, madam, thank you for that. I'd like to turn now to the last two topics of the direct examination, and in that regard can I ask you to go to paragraph 1 -- in paragraph 109 of your statement, you make references to conversations or, communications, in any event, communications with Mr. Tadic about moving Croats, Bosnian Croats, from the Vares-Kakanj area. And now, coming back to Mr. Tadic, this is the Tadic that you were dealing with on the working group that you talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew just one Darinko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the topic of Vares and Kakanj, did this -- did you have this conversation with Mr. Tadic only on one occasion, or did you have a similar conversation with him on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a regular topic. We regularly discussed this topic at all our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who initiated this topic at all of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initiative always came from Mr. Darinko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall what the response of you and your government to Mr. Tadic's position about moving the Bosnian Croats out of the Kakanj Vares area? And for transparency's sake, I refer you to continuing on in your paragraph 109.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that as for this information that I received, well, this information on the problems that Bosnian Croats had, those from the area of Kakanj and Vares that I received from Mr. Tadic, that is. I sent that to the Foreign Ministry of BH and also to the directorate for expellees and refugees of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to this information, these Bosnian Croats had very poor living accommodations. Their accommodation was very poor, they didn't have enough blankets, it was cold, they didn't have enough food. I sent this information further on asking whether this was correct and asking what it was that the government had already done in order to improve their situation. I got assurances in writing and verbally that the government directorate for refugees and expellees had provided additional humanitarian assistance and that it was completely in a position to take care of them, in accordance with what could have been offered to refugees in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know later - and to avoid certain problems, I'll try work backward from there - did it come to your attention later that, in fact, some Bosnian Croats from the Vares area had been relocated somewhere in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this information, we, I mean the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, received this information through the media, namely that a big group had come to Split, that they were at the Poljud stadium. At that moment I had other work to do, but we agreed that Ambassador Turkovic, together with her colleagues, would go to the stadium straight away and get in touch with the expelled Bosnian Croats to see what was expected and what it was that the embassy could objectively do in order to help them. Later on, I also paid a visit. I received information that they were put up at Pinete. I'm not sure how much time had gone by, but it was one of my priorities to go and visit these expelled Bosnian Croats. I spent a day with them, talked to them, received information from them. They confirmed to me and I myself saw that their conditions were pretty good, that they had received humanitarian assistance. So it wasn't really a pressing problem that I had to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said you -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe it was what you are asking. I let you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just on the location, it may or may not be the question Judge Trechsel was asking about, but let me just confirm first of all you did say that you, yourself, ultimately went to one of the locations or perhaps the location where these people were being housed or maintained, a place called Pinete; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought the name was Pinete. I don't know what I wrote. Perhaps there's a printing error, typing mistake. But can you find the paragraph where Pinete comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, you just said it a moment ago, and I'm just responding to what you said in court. Is this an area place in Istria or Istria?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a place which I knew under the name of Pinete with an e, and not Pineta, with an a.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, I'm not sure if that's -- go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What struck me, madam, on page 50, line 5, I think, speak of visiting these expelled Bosnian Croats. Were they actually expelled and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to use the word "expelled." I spent the entire day with them, and I asked them how it came about that they came to Croatia from Bosnia, and their explanation was that they had received information from the HVO according to which a large-scale attack was being planned and that the Mujahedin would arrive with long white beards and that they slaughter people straight away as soon as they enter an area, and following advice from the HVO they agreed to leave the country in an organised fashion and to come to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, they would rather be refugees, than expellees. No one forced them to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the knowledge I had, no. And when I visited them, they already had the recognised status of refugee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May we know exactly when she spoke with them, because I think that it is in connection with your question, Judge Trechsel, when exactly, because she must have taken notes. She takes notes when she meets with Muslims, so why won't she take notes when she meets with Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe it would be a good topic for cross-examination, because it's not exactly what I -- what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look, please, at Exhibit 5960.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, this is a report from the HVO office for displaced persons and refugees, dated at the end of the document, the 26th of October, 1993. The Chamber will recall what happened on the 23rd and 24th of October, 1993. If you look at this document, madam, you will see -- can you just look at it long enough to see what it is? And the question I'm going to ask you is: Is the information reported in this document, or at least some of it, consistent with the information you learned about the movement of these Croats to this area, Pinete, and the information consistent with reports and the conversations you personally had with some of these people at that time? But first of all, before you answer my question, I want you to look at the document long enough so that you can see the information itself.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that this corresponds to the information I had linked to the group of Bosnian Croats who were displaced in Bosnia, and in an organised fashion taken to Croatia and having the status of refugee in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at this document, it's not generated by this woman, and it has nothing to do with her. And again, I object to the form of the question. We asked a question when. Now she's shown a document generated by others, she takes the time to read it, and then she generates an answer, and it doesn't -- it doesn't fit within the rules of trial advocacy to lead a witness in this fashion. We asked when she went. She should have notes. She should have documents of her own, not looking at another document by others that would -- that was generated for a wholly different purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can understand that Mr. Karnavas doesn't like this evidence and it makes him very nervous, and I want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Let me continue first, let me finish and respond to Mr. Karnavas, but the point is -- the point is that the witness in her statement, which has already been tendered and which the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica. Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to say something briefly. The witness just told us that she visited the refugees or expellees or whatever you wish to call them at the stadium in Split, and that several days later, she learnt that those refugees were transferred to Pinete. Now, while the Prosecutor is on the document, I want to point out the second paragraph in both the English and Croatian version where it says that they were refugees who went by ship from Ploce, transported by ship. So it's not the refugees who were at the stadium, and that is why it was improper to link these refugees at the stadium to the information just provided to us by the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's by way of argument, and I object to -- I mean, I was responding to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry I'll let Mr. Scott go first. I'll turn off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can finish, Your Honour, what I was saying before, I'm not sure why I was interrupted. Mr. Karnavas asks questions and talks about notes. There is no requirement that the witness have notes. And again when Mr. Karnavas doesn't like the evidence he thinks of all the reasons why -- irrelevant reasons why it shouldn't be accepted. The witness gave, in her statement, her knowledge about this situation. She said that this came to the attention of the embassy, as it properly would have since these were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had been transported to a foreign country. Therefore, it came to the attention of the embassy. She made inquiries, the embassy made inquiries. She said that Ambassador Turkovic herself visited the group -- this group of people on one occasion and that she herself went and visited them on another occasion, and it is the -- it is quite clear, and all I've done is refer to her then this document, as the Prosecution has done hundreds of times in the past 13 months. It doesn't have to be a document produced by this witness and counsel knows that, to confirm the content of the document exactly consistent with the courtroom practice, and the witness is able to say, "I look at this document. I see the information in it." You will note that it mentions in several places on the second page of the English version, the top of the page for example, Pinete, Pinete, it's on the second -- first paragraph on the second page. It's on the second -- the second page, and et cetera, et cetera. You can see what all happens. And these people arrive. First page says that they were first -- first transported to and arrived in Stolac. An organised convoy transporting about 6.000 displaced Croats from Kakanj and Zenica had been temporarily accommodated in Vares. The convoy comprised about 120 driving units. They were then put that -- they then put the vehicles in a file and separated some of the vehicles transporting 1.500 displaced persons for the Republic of Croatia late -- while the remaining vehicles transported displaced persons starting off half an hour later so as to avoid creating congestion in Capljina where the main reception and distribution of displaced persons was organised. That is in Capljina, which we submit frankly is entirely consistent with other Prosecution evidence. Then it goes on and it talks about that. So counsel can argue all they want and they can put it in cross-examination but the witness has looked at the document and says this is consistent with the information I received when I interviewed these people myself. So I think we're wasting a huge amount of time in pursuing this further and I think the witness testimony stands on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I now just make the comment I was going to make? Your Honour, just briefly to associate myself with the comments made by my learned friends but also to observe that this form of question, this is at page 52 from about line 6 onwards, is unsatisfactory and we have seen it before and I am urging that we don't see it again. It's easy to slip into it, but the form of the question is: Is the information reported in this document or at least some of it consistent with et cetera, et cetera. Your Honour, when we have a document which has got quite a bit of substance in it, and especially when it's not the witness's own document, to ask the question in that form is dangerous in terms of the evidence that the Court will receive. Because Your Honours need to be very clear, if this form of questioning is permitted, very clear, precisely what the witness is able to say is consistent, precisely what she isn't. So the question and the answer together in some way must clearly identify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the response to that, Your Honour, is never been given the opportunity. All we've been doing for the last 15 minutes is arguing procedure and there haven't been any additional questions about -- if I had directed the witness and been more suggestive obviously there would have been an objection to that. So consistent with courtroom practice, I simply asked to look at the document, and if she could agree, confirm at least certain parts of the document which many, many witnesses have done in this courtroom in the past 13 months. Doesn't have to confirm 100 per cent, can confirm some aspects of the document. She's told us what she did, and we're wasting a huge amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the point at all. The particular bits have to be identified. What Mr. Scott says is simply not correct there. The question and answer there -- unless Mr. Scott is going to suggest that there was going to be some elaborate examination that's going to clear it up which would be inconsistent with the way in which this sort of evidence has been approached by the Prosecution in the past, the questioning might -- my submission stands, Your Honour. That form of question is not satisfactory when it leads on to an answer which is not identified very clearly. What Mr. Scott says, we seem to be ad idem on what is required in the end in evidence but we're absolutely not at one on how you get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I believe that you've been to Pinete. That's what I understood. Is that the case? Yes or no? There in Pinete you met with some Croatian refugees. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These Croatian refugees, were they from the Kakanj or Zenica region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kakanj and Vares. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well. We have a document here where mention is made of refugees from Kakanj and Zenica who arrived in Pinete. It is also stated that Mr. Boban came to visit them on the 22nd of October, 1993. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a final follow-up. You mentioned some minutes ago now that when you talked to the people at this location, these people from Vares, you mentioned they had been told by the HVO that they had essentially -- they'd better leave because the Mujahedin were on the way, so to speak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did any of those people ever tell you in those conversations --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, during the cross-examination you will have the opportunity to respond. I note that every time the Prosecution puts questions that might be difficult for you, you intervene immediately, but please let the Prosecution proceed, because you would not be very pleased if they proceeded the same way as you do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I have nothing against the answer given by this witness. I don't think that it will be a problem for the Defence to clear up the details, and I consider that I'm on my feet on very rare occasions, but I think this is the right moment to draw your attention to the following: That this document was compiled on the 26th of October, 1993, and that roughly speaking that is eight or nine days before the fall of Vares and before the departure of the population of Vares from the town of Vares, and the witness -- the reason the witness mentions about the Mujahedin are what the Bosniak witnesses have told us allegedly as an explanation they gave by the population of Vares. So I think that my intervention would help clarify the meaning of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Madam, my final question to you that I was beginning to put to you was when you spoke to these people from -- the Bosnian Croats from Vares, when you spoke to them directly, did any of them tell you that they had actually seen any Mujahedin or this is only what the HVO had told them?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only what they told them from the HVO. Nobody confirmed having seen the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Final topic, madam. In paragraph 112 of your statement you talk about a humanitarian convoy that you say had been held up for seven months.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with humanitarian convoys, let me also, before putting some follow-up questions to you, let me also ask you to look at Exhibit 10049. You have that, madam?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the second paragraph of the document which says: "Due to the blockade of the border and the prevailing situation in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina, all inland-bound movement of people and goods was suspended on the 16th of April, 1993 ..." Can you confirm to the Chamber whether you and the embassy that you worked in at the time, were you aware that this blockage had been put into place as of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally knew that a blockade was put into place, but I didn't have the exact date of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did you first become involved in efforts to try to get this convoy freed? You say in paragraph 112 it had been some seven months. And this was September. So can we understand that this had been going on since at least February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was faced with these problems after appointment to the working group, which was supposed to deal with issues of status for refugees and humanitarian aid. And it was established after an agreement reached between Izetbegovic and Tudjman in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then -- but you -- in paragraph 112, I'm just trying to get the timing of this as much as we can given various objections have been raised before, as you say: "It was well known that a convoy humanitarian aid was stopped for about seven months in Split at TTS terminal," and I think you mentioned TTS yesterday, if I'm not mistaken, in another context. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that part. And what I can say is that what it says in paragraph 112 is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as we read on in your statement, paragraph 113, paragraph 114 and following, did you have conversations in your meetings with Mr. Tadic, this same Mr. Tadic, and Mr. Zubak about getting this convoy released?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to cover all the details that are in your statement, but can you just tell the Chamber, can you recall whether that convoy in fact was ever allowed to go on its way and reach its destination in -- in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the agreement, oral and written, reached by this working group the convoy was ultimately released, and it reached its final destination, and UNPROFOR reported from all the check-points as to whether the convoy had passed by a section of the route that it was supposed to pass through to reach its final destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, I think that concludes the direct examination. I want to thank you on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor for coming to The Hague and giving your testimony, and I wish you a safe trip home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, fine. The examination-in-chief is now over. We have about 30 minutes before the next break. Who would like to start on the Defence? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, and Your Honours. I was wondering whether we should take the break now because I'm going to need two or three minutes to set up. Otherwise, I could start, but it will take time. It doesn't matter. I'll leave it to you. Either way, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you need some time to get ready, so we will break now and we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. Now, as I understand your thesis, the office of the displaced persons and refugees of the republic of the Croatia was the state's logistics for the ethnic cleansing of Muslims, based on your thesis. That would be one part of it, would it not be?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in definitions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Part of your thesis is also that the refugees were kept in -- in camps, and they were kept there by the army or the special police. That's also part of your thesis; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to the use of the word "thesis". I think the evidence -- the witness has come to give her evidence under oath, and I don't think there's any reason to be so argumentative at this stage and suggest something other than the witness's evidence, not a thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's your evidence. It's your evidence that the refugees were kept there by the Republic of Croatia. They were kept in camps, and they were kept by the army and the police. Correct? That's part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Part of your evidence is that the Muslim refugees did not have a right to an education in the Republic of Croatia other than what you were providing. In other words, that the Republic of Croatia was denying Muslim refugees the right to an education. That's part of your evidence, is it not, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My evidence is that refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were Muslims could not exercise their right to a regular education in the schools of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it also be part of your evidence that the humanitarian aid was spent by the Republic of Croatia in an irregular way? And I think you touched upon it yesterday when you were making complaints how they wanted to fix infrastructure as opposed to provide aid for Muslim refugees. Is that part of your evidence as well, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some comments in relation to certain documents, and I interpreted them orally. Could you perhaps help me? Could you tell me what the document that we're discussing is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're going to go through various documents, but first let's talk a little bit about your background. Now, as I understand it, when you were selected to go to -- to the Republic of Croatia, you had no prior experience in this particular field. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, from your own statement, your own admissions, when you went to the Republic of Croatia to be engaged in organising this humanitarian operation that you were involved in along with others, that you had no official instructions.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had been an economist; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Working in the tourist industry?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And also you had some experience in Energoinvest, I believe, and as I understand it, all or most of your experience had been in marketing. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with -- when you -- when you arrived in the Republic of Croatia the war had been going on for some time, correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One-third of Croatia was occupied?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't expect me to confirm percentage points, figures, et cetera. I assume that that is the case, but I personally would not wish to engage in speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A large part of Croatia was occupied.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as a result of that occupation that had -- that had occurred sometime before your arrival, there was a large segment of the Croatian population from the Republic of Croatia that were displaced; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with a figure between 300.000, 400.000, 500.000, would that be a figure that was thrown around by the international community at the time and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated by the time that you arrived and while you were there approximately 300.000 refugees came from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Those were our estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if my math is correct, whatever area of Croatia that was not occupied had to take care of anywhere from 600 to 800.000 refugees and displaced persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it from -- you saw my interventions yesterday. I take it if I were to ask you concretely whether the embassy that you worked for, whether they had done any studies to see to what extent the Republic of Croatia could absorb these sorts of numbers of persons needing humanitarian assistance, the answer would be that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not engaged in economic studies. At least I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But one would think that at least before assuming that a particular government was not doing enough in assisting refugees who are coming from another country, as well as taking care of their own needy displaced persons, one would know more or less whether the existing infrastructure was able to manage that large influx of people that needed humanitarian assistance. You didn't make any inquiries, did you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't making any inquiries, and I was not coming to any conclusions as to whether enough was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we talk about the two refugee centres that have been the focal point of our discussion over the past two days, it is fair to say that Croatia, with its islands and its past tourist industry, which was rather lively prior to the war, used various places such as hotels, resort areas and what have you, to accommodate displaced persons and refugees. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, one would say that virtually no space was not scrutinised to see whether -- no free space, that is, whether it could be used in some way, some fashion, some capacity, to take care of the needy displaced persons and refugees that Croatia had to absorb in such a short time under such a volatile circumstance?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we -- let's speak about the first refugee centre, and you have to forgive me for my pronunciation. I've been working on it for six years but I don't seem to -- my B/C/S doesn't seem to improve. The first place I want to talk about is Gasinci. Now, this -- this centre was located in the north of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not far away from Djakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The centre was receiving refugees fleeing from BiH northwards.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that they were fleeing northwards. I know that the centre was receiving refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, prior to the war you must have been aware, or you must have become aware at some point that this, the Gasinci, was used as a training centre for high-ranking JNA officers. Correct? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally really did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you were not aware that this had been a training centre for high-ranking JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But needless to say, for those of us who did not grow up in the former Yugoslavia, it's fair to say that high-ranking JNA officers had a particular status in Tito's Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's exactly what I knew too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, would it surprise you to learn that that centre had significant and quality accommodation capacities?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be surprised. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That it had medical facilities? Again keeping in mind what its intended use was, and I'm saying prior to the war, that it had medical facilities. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about this facility before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't know, then, that this facility also had all the necessities to receive a large number of people since, after all, this was a training centre? You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it throughout the entire time you were there on behalf of the embassy looking after the refugees, you never became aware of what this place was or had been at one point or time -- one point in time? You never became aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know whether the cost of the food and the other infrastructural costs were being covered by the Croatian government? Were you aware of that or -- or do you know?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had different information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is your information such that -- would be that the Croatian government did not, I underscore did not through the office of displaced persons and refugees provide the costs for food and other infrastructural costs at this centre? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that is not what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say, then, at least part of the costs, if you're not willing to say all of the costs, part of the costs for food on other infrastructural costs were borne by the Republic of Croatia? Were you be -- would you acknowledge that? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot discuss that, because I really do not know. I'm not aware of this information as to whether they had any costs and to what extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, they would have had costs if they were trying to feed all these refugees that are living there. Somebody has pay for those costs; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And surely you're not suggesting that those costs were borne by some other entity some other government exclusively, and that the Croatian government provided no costs, provided no benefits to these refugees that were -- that they were responsible for. You're not trying to say that, are you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say by way of giving evidence on that subject is that part of the costs were covered by a humanitarian organisation, and that is the only thing I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would it be fair to say that additional accommodation capacities were constructed in cooperation with donations by humanitarian organisations? Would it be fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me get this straight then. While you were there, while you were visiting, you were not able to see any construction ongoing or any new construction having been completed. You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived all the construction had been completed. All the houses had been finished, and refugees were living in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it would be fair to say that by the time you arrived there had been quite a few refugees coming into the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because you arrived, I believe, sometime in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived on the 1st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1st of March, 1993. And could you just tell us, if you recall, based on the events of the break-up of Yugoslavia, about what time, what period of time would it have been that the Republic of Croatia began receiving displaced persons and/or refugees as a result of what was happening in the former Yugoslavia? What year? And what month, if you know.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I was in Croatia in September 1992, and I know. I can testify to the fact that already then there were quite a few refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia. I was on an official trip. I was going through Croatia, and I can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that maybe even earlier than that, a year earlier than that, or six months earlier than that you had refugees and displaced persons occupying various places, centres in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it is logical that this can be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be also logical then to also say that when you have large amounts of people coming in all of a sudden that the infrastructure gets worn down from usage?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so given that you came in March 1991 [sic], and given that you hadn't been to this place prior to that, if I understand you correctly, since you did not know what it was prior used for, that you don't know what the conditions were of this particular refugee centre when refugees and displaced persons first begun to arrive; correct? And you arrived in 1993, the transcript should say on line 7 on page 70.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The information I had about that was only the information I received from other persons present then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you're not suggesting that while you were there that the special -- that the special police were also staying in those premises, the very same premises where the refugees and displaced persons were staying? That is not your testimony, or is it?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about the Gasinci refugee centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to say that at the same time there was special police in Gasinci while the refugees were there, and I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, let's talk about the other centre, Obonjan. Obonjan. I'll get there one of these days. Okay. Now, I guess another possibility for refugees to exit Bosnia and Herzegovina would be from the south of the country, and that would have put them sort of in that location where they would have easy access to get to Obonjan Island; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I wouldn't like to go into geography. I'm not really an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Had you been to that island before the war?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that prior to the war that that had been a former Scout centre, that it had a former Scout centre over there?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand, it was called the Island of Youth, something like that. And I would suspect that since this was a centre for Scouts that it, too, had the capacity, already the infrastructure, to handle large crowds, a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that your assumption is wrong, because the management of the centre kept complaining about the inappropriate infrastructure all the time. So the management themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go step-by-step, you see. That's why I asked you by the time you get there, almost two years, you have these centres receiving people. And we agreed that in that amount of time, with that influx of people, there's bound to be wear and tear. You know that from living in your own house. You can paint it one day, six months later there's wear and tear if you've got kids running around.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my knowledge indicates that refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina could have started arriving in Croatia only starting from the spring of 1992. So we're not talking about the previous two years but the previous one year. The one year prior to my arrival, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we also talked about displaced persons. But in any event, this place being a centre for Scouts, for the youth, is it not a fact that this -- that this island would have had facilities to accommodate large numbers of people already on the island?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not a fact. At the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when I arrived there were tents on the island.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, you said -- now, in order to get to that island you have to take a ferry boat; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The alternative was to rent smaller private boats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And we're talking about two to three nautical miles. We're not talking about going out on the open sea. We're talking about two to three nautical miles, are we not, between this island and, say, Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how many miles it is. I don't have a feeling for that, but I know that the journey was about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You had ferry boats going back and forth?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were regular lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Refugees that were -- that came there came primarily from Split? Originally they were from Split and they would make it over to the island?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I thought you were -- you spent a lot of time with them questioning them. You didn't ask them, "By which way did you get to the island? Did they helicopter you? Did you swim? Did you take a ferry?" You didn't ask any of them, like, from which direction you came?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they came from Sibenik on a ferry to Obonjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you're not aware whether they were coming from Split?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Split was overcrowded, was it not, with refugees and displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was also rather close to the front line, as it were? I mean not right on it, but close?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is not speculation, I could agree. To my mind, it was close to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now, do you know whether some of the refugees that made it to this island came by way of the navy? You know, they came by ship, naval ships?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all arrived on ferry boats. All the refugees arrived in ferry boats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. All right. Let's move on then. We'll move on to something else. Just on this -- well -- on education I just want to ask you one question, because yesterday you mentioned about having a certificate of baptism or the ksrni list or something like that.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's something you get from the Catholic church, I would imagine, or from the church; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But up until that time, at least in order to enroll into school you needed a birth certificate, did you not? I mean, when you would take your child to be registered in school, the school would require something from the government, not something from the church; right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my country, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what about in Croatia? You were there, and you said that this policy was put into existence. I looked through all the documents and I haven't seen a single document and you haven't produced anything as far as a law, a decree, a decision, something, that would verify what it is that you claim, that is that in order for a child to be registered for public education in Croatia during this period, I think it was 1992, 1993, that they would require, they would need a krsni list, some kind of a religious document, a certificate of baptism which obviously would not have been available to Muslim children, therefore the discriminatory factor. Now, do you have anything? Have you produced anything to the Prosecutor that perhaps he just failed or forgot to disclose to us?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to the decree of the government of the Republic of Croatia that was published in their Official Gazette which we in the office for refugees had, and I probably attached it to my report sent out to UN organisations and government institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't remember whether I saw it during these past two days in the documents that I looked through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you correctly, and correct me if I'm wrong, that there was -- there was a law in force on the right of displaced persons and refugees, and that's where you would find that -- that passage, that requirement, or is this some kind of other law, the law on education, which of the two? Because frankly, and before you answer let me just tell you, I've scoured the documents, I've looked all over, and I haven't found anything that you've written complaining to anybody, regarding this particular issue, that is, the certificate of baptism, other than, of course, what you put into your report which we have no evidence to verify. So could you help us out here?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave my statement, I consulted my documents, the ones I had, and in my reports you had numbers, the documents to which I referred, the Official Gazette issues and numbers, and I think it might be helpful to take a look at the statement or report that was compiled for certain institutions in order to try and find which decree or law I refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ever consult the law on the rights of displaced persons and refugees, because that would have covered at least the rights of the refugees and displaced persons that were in Croatia. I would assume that you would have had that and you would have been consulting with it on your day-to-day affairs. Did you have that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did do that, but I was fully conscious of the fact that I wasn't a legal expert. I did not study law. So I took on a legal expert in my department, and he was involved throughout that time with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So that legal expert would have been at least able to look at that law, analyse it to some extent, and then based on his analysis point out what rights displaced persons and refugees had in Croatia; correct? All right.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We can move on a little bit. If we could look at document 1D 01232. And this is a document -- it's a decree law on displaced persons and refugees, and this is from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, we could see -- the number is 1D 01232. 1232.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to the very last page, we see that it was signed by Dr. Ganic. I'm sure you know who he was at the time. And the date is 6 October 1992. This would have been prior to your engagement in the capacity in which you were in Croatia; correct? This would have been prior to your working for the Croatian embassy -- I mean the Bosnian embassy in -- in Croatia. And I should say Bosnia and Herzegovina embassy.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. The date predates my arrival to the embassy of the BHR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you had been working -- you had been working in the office of refugees in Sarajevo in 1992, so surely, surely you must have been aware of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I worked there, but it is not correct that I must have been aware of the existence of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You worked in the office of refugees in Sarajevo from August 1992 to March 1993, or the end of February 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an employee of the directorate, but for two and a half months during that period of time I was absent. I was out of the country. So I didn't necessarily have to know that this law had been enacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you ever look at the law at that point in time, at that period, so for instance, when you were -- and I'll tell you why I'm asking the question. When you were in the Republic of Croatia perhaps you could turn to Mr. Rebic and say, see what a law we have in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a country that's involved in war and here you are, only part of your country is occupied and you're not in the same condition. Why don't you compare and contrast what rights we provide refugees and displaced persons versus what you're doing over here? Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to look at a couple of things very quickly. If we could go at Article 20. And before we discuss it, it's fair to say that there is a difference between a displaced person and a refugee; correct? And obviously you would know the distinction. I'll walk you through the article step-by-step, but I'm wondering whether OP the top of your memory whether you know the distinction between a displaced person and refugee. There is a distinction; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at Article 20, we see under 1, we see this -- well, we see, "the status of a person recognised, the status of a displaced person and/or refugee shall cease -- shall cease." "1. By a decision of the displaced person and refugee welfare staff of the municipality according to his/her permanent place of residence, when the reasons for which he/she fled his/her permanent place of residence ceases to exist." So at least from Article 20.1, it would seem that under this particular law, once you can return to your place of origin you cease having the status of displaced person or refugee. Of course there's some other conditions, but this is -- we can see that from here; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Of course number 2, it says: "On the basis of his or her own decision to return to his/her permanent place of residence." So, in other words, free will. Irrespective of whether it's safe or not, every individual has the free will, even to put themselves in harm's way in order to return to their place of origin; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct that this was written and every person has the right to free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And then we look at number 3: "If he/she refuses the offered accommodation and/or other forms of organised assistance." In other words -- let me give you a concrete example. If, for instance, refugees may be in a hotel on a resort area and now the government wishes to relocate them into tents where other refugees around the world especially normally live in, and if a refugee or displaced person refuses that offer, then they could lose their status. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct, and I did know about that while I performed my duties as attache.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to go down to Article -- oh. We'll go to Article 21. And if we look at Article 21, we don't have to spend too much time on it, but under 1 it says: "The refugee status of a person from the war-ridden area of the border republics of the former Yugoslavia who have been recognised that status shall cease: "1. If it can be concluded from his/her conduct that he/she is not abiding by the legal order of the republic." And again let me give you a concrete example. In other words, if somebody is committing crimes while they're a guest as a refugee or a displaced person -- well, here it talks about refugee, they lose their status. So if somebody comes from another country as a refugee, they commit crimes, they could lose their status; correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What you read out is correct, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again if we look at number 3 because this relates to refugees: "If he/she refuses the offered organised accommodation and other forms of organised assistance." It somewhat repeats Article 21. Then if we go to Article 22 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just to interrupt just briefly for the record, I just want to question the relevance of this material since the only statute that would be relevant to this witness's evidence would be the laws in effect in the Republic of Croatia at the time. She was dealing with refugees and displaced persons physically located in Croatia, and I don't know why we're spending all this time talking about the law in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist. I can assist, Your Honour, and I welcome that intervention by the Prosecutor. I'm surprised that he's on his feet on that intervention, because -- because -- thank you. We've heard that we had reverse ethnic cleansing today. You see, a couple weeks ago we're trying to get rid of Muslims and send them all over the place. Now we're trying to take these Muslims and send them back to -- to Bosnia. So it seems that the authorities, no matter what they do, are damned. Now, there are certain obligations for refugees. You had a Prosecutor who was saying they weren't getting any education. Their document, in the statement, they're complaining about how they were not given sufficient accommodations, or they wanted to move them to tents because they wanted to stay in hotels or other resort areas. And the whole purpose of that -- of that direct examination was to show discrimination, was to show that somehow this is part of the pattern of joint criminal enterprise. Also, if we go on a little bit, just a little bit, we'll see that those who are of military-age men who are conscripts also have an obligation. In fact we'll see, perhaps with this witness or another witness, that they were required and Bosnia was pushing, Bosnia-Herzegovina was pushing the Republic of Croatia to send back their men of military age in order to assist in the war, in the war effort. Then if we go to Article 25, we'll see and compare it with Article 26, displaced persons are entitled to schooling, or under Article 26, refugees are not entitled to schooling. And we'll have some other evidence, but the reason I'm showing this is because for contextual purposes. If Croatia doesn't do enough, then obviously it's engaged in a joint criminal enterprise, no matter what it does. And so I think this is relevant, because they have opened the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to respond. It's a rather long argument in front of the witness, and I think it's -- I think it's inappropriate, but, but, I am going to ask to also respond to it fairly as well. Number one, I don't think Mr. Karnavas should mischaracterise the Prosecution position. The Prosecution position is that, yes, these various devices and policies were used to facilitate and carry out forms of ethnic cleansing and keep Muslims from, in fact, being returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was said the evidence was on various of these points was that the Muslims, despite what someone might have said on paper and sometimes they did and sometimes they didn't, but the real effect was the Muslims couldn't, in fact, return for a number of reasons. One, why would they go back to the very place where they had just been arrested and had their homes burned down and been detained? Why would they go back under those conditions? Number two, when they tried to go back to other parts of ABiH-controlled territory in Bosnia, the HVO would not give them passage through HVO-controlled territory. So it's fine -- it's all well and good to say well, in fact, we were happy to send Muslims back but they couldn't go back and the people knew that. It would have been known to anyone involved in this situation. Number two, number two, this is nothing more -- I mean, now it's transparent that this is nothing more than another form of tu quoque. I mean, you know, well, so let's not look at the Croatian law which presumably all the counsel across from me can access the laws in Zagreb and what the Croatian law was at the time. Let's not put that in front of witness. Instead, let's look at the law that didn't apply to people in Croatia, and that's -- we now know the real ulterior reason is not to show the right document to the witness but to engage in a form of tu quoque. It's completely irrelevant and the evidence of the witness as opposed to Mr. Karnavas's characterisation of all the reasons that in fact the Muslims could not go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina for all the reasons put in their way, even if they had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may reply very briefly. First of all, unlike Mr. Scott, I cannot and choose not to try my entire case with every witness. I think that's what he's trying to do and that's why I object so much to some of the evidence trying to come in through various witnesses who are not competent to testify. That's number one. Number two, number two, let's keep in mind that prior to 1991, you had one country called Yugoslavia. It then breaks up. Now these are very special conditions, this whole war thing, and we want to criticise the Republic of Croatia. Yesterday, I put a question to the Prosecutor where he named Mr. Rebic as part of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He did and it was heard all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Find me the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So here we have the Prosecutor, they want it both ways. Now, I'm entitled to put my case, my case, not his case, one step at a time. So not only am I trying to refute his theory, which I think is bogus, but also I'm trying to do so by advancing my theory, which I think is contextually accurate when you look at the circumstances. So for instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can respond to my arguments but he cannot mischaracterise the record and he cannot say the evidence is something that it's not. Of course he can conduct a fair and effective cross-examination of the witness, and the Prosecution is never on its feet or objecting when it deems that there is a fair, albeit sometimes aggressive, cross-examination. But when Mr. Karnavas mischaracterises the evidence or mischaracterises the Prosecution position, then indeed I will be on my feet to correct that and object, and that's what I'm doing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I've got the record right here, if the Court would like to be reminded of it. It was yesterday's transcript, and the page numbering I may not -- page numbering went away during a break but I think it's around page 60-ish, anyway, I can quote the words. "Mr. Scott: Your Honour the, indictment I'm just having the chance to try to look at it but clearly it is a part of the Prosecution case that since counsel asked me directly, and I'll respond directly, yes, that this was part of the ethnic cleansing of Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Herceg-Bosna area." And that was in direct response to a question from Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, "Mr. Scott, is Mr. Rebic a member of the joint criminal enterprise?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my response was not to Mr. Rebic but that to the -- nature of the joint criminal enterprise. Show me -- sorry, sorry, when I'm -- when I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When I'm going to be personally attacked and said that I said something on the record, I never said that Mr. Rebic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise. I responded to the president's question by saying, Yes, it is a component of the Prosecution case that the joint criminal enterprise involved the movement of people to Croatia, deportation, which is charged in the indictment, and conditions such that including conditions by which these people could not return to their home countries. That's what I said, and again I did not say on the record and I stand by it despite what Mr. Murphy has just said, I did not say, and Mr. Rebic was a member of the JCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So is Mr. Rebic not a member of the joint criminal enterprise? Maybe that's the question that he should answer today. Because if you look at the law on joint criminal enterprise he is either aiding and abetting particular crimes, because you cannot aid and abet a joint criminal enterprise, or he is a member of the joint criminal enterprise, or he's a direct physical perpetrator of the joint criminal enterprise. But no matter how you slice it and dice it given his position and given the arguments that's what they asserted. And so I'm entitled to go into all this area because I'm trying to put it into context. It's a step-by-step process. We have months to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you're perfectly entitled to put your case as you see fit, but the four Judges you have before you are legal specialists, of course, and they wonder why irrespective of the law on displaced persons and refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we wonder why you don't have a text law related to displaced persons and refugees in the Republic of Croatia? I leafed through your binder. I found a statute or a text related to the situation in Denmark, probably quite interesting, but what would even be more interesting for us would be a text related to Croatia, because the lady here was in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for asking that question. Again let me remind the Bench that first and foremost the Prosecution has the burden of proof not the Defence. It is not for me to bring in evidence that they should be bringing. Secondly, should I decide to put on a case and should I think that is necessary, I will do so with my own witness. So at this point the Trial Chamber cannot be directing me as to what my case should be. Moreover, I think it's a little unfair for the Trial Chamber to presume to know what my case is because I'm doing it step-by-step. I'm putting a little -- a little stone step, you know, one by one. Eventually you'll see it. Maybe you won't see it, but -- maybe I won't be able to prove whatever it is I'm trying to prove, but I do not have the burden and I got my answer. My answer was this person was there in situ for a year or a year and a half, whatever and never bothered to look at the law. Doesn't have it, doesn't cite it. And that's why I said yesterday her entire testimony is based on anecdotal, "I heard this," "somebody told me," nothing concrete. She says that there is -- there is this decision regarding children. In order to be enrolled they need something from the church. Where is it? Where is it in the law? Where is the document where you've complained about it? I don't have it. I don't know where it is. So I don't have to produce these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think maybe there's a misunderstanding. This is not about what your case should be. It is about the question, Why on earth do we go lengthily through a legislative text which is not the one applicable to the situation the witness is talking about? The situation that the witness has not been working, mainly, has not been working with this legislation but with a different one, and it is really not quite clear why we spend all this time on this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on. For the sake of -- I don't want to argue the point. I'll move only. If the Trial Chamber doesn't want to hear this type of evidence I'll bring it in my case, my own case, because I think, Your Honour, with all due respect, this case cannot be tried in a vacuum. That's my whole point. You know, you had a country that broke up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karnavas, that is not sufficient as an explanation why you go into this by just saying it cannot be tried in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We stand to be convinced, but if you do not succeed then indeed better go off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will go off, but again I remind Your Honours you don't have a dossier. You didn't spend a year and a half, two years, preparing for this trial, I have. But in any event we will be submitting this document in, and I will just ask the Trial Chamber to note that on Article 25 and 26, Article 25 does provide for displaced persons to be -- to get schooling where refugees are not provided for any schooling. And it seems a little double standardish to say that somebody coming from -- from Bosnia to say we demand that you provide deluxe accommodations when in their own law they say if you refuse you lose your status. But I'll move on Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, no one said deluxe accommodations. And again if there's any further questions about this statute -- this Rule 1D 01232, we will indeed object. I was being very patient before because I assumed perhaps we wouldn't stay on it very long, but I completely share the Chamber's view that this is completely irrelevant, and I am sure Mr. Karnavas and I may disagree about a lot of things, but I am completely confident that if Mr. Karnavas would have wanted to find the appropriate Croatian law with all the assistance of the Croatian lawyers across the room, I'm quite confident he could have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I really think we should let Mr. Karnavas continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you. I appreciate the guidance from the Prosecution who bears the further for proving all the allegations they are making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, on that point that reminds me of another legitimate point I want to raise. And I'm not going to let it go, I'm not going to let it slide by because again it's unfair to Mr. Karnavas. He says that this witness impeaches the witness's credibility or that the truth of what she's saying by saying, They haven't produced a policy that says there was a policy of questioning. Well, at the moment her evidence on that it's unimpeached. There is no evidence to the contrary. This woman came in here under oath and she said while I was in the embassy in Zagreb, a policy or law was put to this effect. There is no evidence in this courtroom to the contrary. And as long -- it doesn't matter how many times Mr. Karnavas gets on his feet and says, Why haven't they produced a document? It doesn't matter she is unimpeached. Her testimony on this point is unimpeached, and there has been nothing to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour I don't want to get into a discussion on evidence. I would love to, especially on this. We have hearsay evidence coming in and if it -- if it's not impeached it comes in. I dare say Mr. Scott should read Judge May's book on evidence before the Tribunal. It might assist him. Now if we could go to the next document 1D 01576. 1D 01576. It's a letter from Mr. -- Professor Dr. Rebic. August 30, 1993. And it's short so I'll read it. It's addressed to -- it's from the office of the displaced persons and refugees of the government of the Republic of Croatia to the embassy of the RBiH in the Republic of Croatia. "Dear sirs, "It is an honour to inform you that for the purpose of extending the refugee status of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the social welfare centres of the Republic of Croatia do not," I underscore that, "do not require any type of certificate from your side. This must be a result of lack of information from individual officers in the centres. "On August 30, 1993, the centres were given instructions to extend refugee status for another three months to those persons already having this status and not being able to return to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Question: Ma'am, were you aware of this letter dated August 30, 1993? It calls for a yes or no. And I believe it's from your -- your own documents, in fact. You must have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of all the facts, but I cannot claim whether I actually saw the letter or not. I'm aware of all the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Would it be -- would it surprise you if I were to tell you that this came from the batch of documents that you provided to the Prosecutor or somebody provided to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and incidentally your office was in the embassy? Madam, your office, was that in the embassy?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first few months the office was in the embassy physically, but later on it was at another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And speaking of that embassy, because you were asked a question yesterday about how many people were employed there, and I believe you indicated that there were some 20 people, perhaps more, that were working for the consulate. How many of those people were Bosnian Croats or Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina? How many were employed?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You worked there for a year and you didn't know that you had any colleagues that were from Bosnia and Herzegovina that were of Croatian origin? All right. What about Serbs? Any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, okay. Do you know -- so I take it from your answers you didn't -- within your own department dealing with refugees, and some of those refugees would have been of Croatian origin, there wasn't one single solitary Croat from Bosnia and Herzegovina working with you. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. How big of a staff did you have? I don't want to take too much time on this, but how big of a staff did you have that you didn't know whether among your entire staff -- and remember you said yesterday, the entire embassy had 20 people so you couldn't have that big of a staff. So among all of your staff, you didn't know whether any of them were of Croatian origin?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only six to seven staff members. I knew that some of them had citizenship of the Republic of Croatia. I don't know whether they declared themselves as Croats, Muslims, or Serbs. I assert that that is not something that we discussed among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. But just one last question on that issue. Suffice it to say, from the name you can sometimes tell, not always, sometimes, whether somebody is a Muslim or a non-Muslim.
